title: Carbon tax

definition.text: A carbon tax is a tax charged on the carbon released when goods and services are produced.

facts.text: It aims to make the hidden social costs of carbon emissions visible by raising the price of fossil fuels.
Higher prices cut demand for high-emission goods and push producers to make them less carbon-intensive.
Unlike command-and-control rules that cap each polluter, a carbon tax lets market forces find the cheapest way to cut pollution.
Its design turns on two choices: how high to set the tax, usually based on the social cost of carbon, and what to do with the revenue.
In its simplest form it covers only CO2, but it can also tax methane or nitrous oxide by their CO2-equivalent warming potential.
Research shows carbon taxes do often reduce emissions; a 2015 British Columbia study found cuts of 5–15% with negligible overall economic effects.
As of 2019 carbon taxes had been implemented or scheduled in 25 countries, and 46 countries priced carbon in some form.
David Gordon Wilson first proposed this type of tax in 1973.

contested_note: Studies find it can hit poor households harder than rich ones, but Gilbert Metcalf disputed that it would be regressive in the US.

definition.text: A carbon tariff, or border carbon adjustment, is a charge on imports according to the carbon emitted in making them.

facts.text: Its usual aim is to prevent carbon leakage from states that have no carbon price.
High-carbon imports that might face one include coal-fired electricity, blast-furnace iron and steel, and fertilizer from the Haber process.
Only California applies one for electricity, while the European Union and the United Kingdom will apply them from 2026 and 2027.
Carbon credits, carbon taxes and Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms are all forms of carbon pricing.
Likely targets include electricity from coal-fired power stations, iron and steel from blast furnaces, and fertilizer from the Haber process.
California has applied one to imported electricity since 2011, and the EU and UK apply them from 2026 and 2027.
Border adjustment is considered an economically efficient fix for leakage, but it might disguise trade protectionism.
Current WTO rules may prohibit some types, and the WTO has not reached a conclusion.

title: Environmental tax

definition.text: An environmental tax, also called an ecotax or green tax, is a tax on activities that harm the environment, meant to steer people toward cleaner alternatives.

facts.text: Ecotaxes are a kind of Pigouvian tax, a tax on goods whose making or use imposes costs on others.
They can address the failure of free markets to limit environmental harm, and can complement or replace command-and-control regulation.
Ireland's €0.22 plastic bag tax cut plastic bags' share of litter from 5% to 0.13% in 14 years and raised over €200 million.
Because the poor spend more of their income on consumption, taxes on consumption can be regressive.
Germany enacted an ecotax through laws in 1998, 1999 and 2002, cutting income taxes so the total tax burden stayed constant.
In 2018 China replaced its 1979 Pollutant Discharge Fee with an environmental protection tax.
Economists critical of degrowth argue that price incentives through environmental taxes or tradable permits are much more effective.

contested_note: Some green tax shift proposals have been criticized as regressive, falling harder on poorer households.

definition.text: Environmental taxes are usually sorted into four categories: energy, transport, pollution and resource taxes.

facts.text: Energy taxes, levied on producing, distributing or using fuels such as coal, oil and gas, are the most common environmental taxes worldwide.
Transport taxes, the second most notable kind, fall on vehicle ownership and use, such as registration taxes based on weight, fuel efficiency or emissions.
Pollution taxes cover measured emissions to air and water and the management of waste and noise.
Resource taxes on extracting water, forests or wildlife are the least common; depletion is usually handled by government fees instead.

definition.text: An emissions tax makes each emitter pay a charge for every tonne of greenhouse gas it releases, while an energy tax is charged on the fuels themselves.

facts.text: Emissions taxes and energy taxes are two taxes closely related to the carbon tax.
A carbon tax encourages using less fuel but does not reward cutting emissions by other means such as carbon capture and storage, so it is not a perfect substitute for an emissions tax.

definition.text: A fuel tax, also called a gas tax or fuel duty, is an excise tax charged on the sale of fuel, usually transport fuel.

facts.text: Its revenue is often earmarked for transport projects, making it a kind of user fee; elsewhere it goes to general revenue.
It is sometimes used as an ecotax, and fuel taxes can act as an implicit price on carbon.
The IPCC, International Energy Agency, IMF and World Bank have urged governments to raise gasoline taxes to cover the social and environmental costs of its use.
Agencies such as the US Internal Revenue Service often regard fuel taxes as regressive.
Between 2003 and 2015 more countries raised gasoline taxes than cut them, yet the global mean gasoline tax fell because low-tax countries consumed more.
Indirect carbon prices such as fuel taxes are far more common than carbon taxes; in 2021 the OECD found 67 of 71 assessed countries had some fuel tax.
Jet fuel for commercial flights within the EU cannot be taxed under the 2003 Energy Taxation Directive.

definition.text: A Pigouvian tax is a tax on a market activity that imposes costs on third parties, known as negative externalities.

facts.text: Ideally the tax equals the external marginal cost of the harm, correcting a market failure.
When outsiders bear part of the cost, the private cost understates the total and the market produces too much of the activity.
It is named after the English economist Arthur Cecil Pigou, who argued in The Economics of Welfare (1920) for taxing producers whose private and social costs diverge.
The tax shifts the producer's marginal private cost up by the size of the externality, so output falls toward the socially best level.
Taxing emissions themselves can reach the long-run social optimum, while taxing proxies such as output may fail to.
For positive externalities the mirror policy is a Pigouvian subsidy, such as subsidies for flu vaccines or research.
Governments often use it because it has relatively low transaction costs compared with regulation or subsidies.
Environmental taxes, including carbon and fuel taxes, are a classic example of Pigouvian taxes.

title: Double dividend hypothesis

definition.text: The double dividend hypothesis holds that swapping environmental taxes for other taxes, without changing total revenue, could deliver two benefits at once.

facts.text: The first dividend is a cleaner environment; the second is a more efficient tax system from cutting distorting taxes such as income tax.
Tullock first advanced the idea in 1967, and David Pearce popularized the term in 1991.
Fullerton and Metcalf note that every $1 raised in taxes puts a $1.35 burden on the economy; the second dividend aims to remove part of that excess.
Bovenberg and de Mooij proposed a 'tax interaction effect' that could make the second dividend negative.

Goulder (1994) split it into a weak form, that cutting distorting taxes beats lump-sum refunds, and a strong form, that the reform lowers overall economic cost; the strong form needs special conditions.
Fullerton and Metcalf concluded it cannot be established as a whole; each case depends on existing taxes and where the revenue goes.

contested_note: Economists disagree on whether the second, tax-efficiency dividend is positive or negative.

definition.text: The tax interaction effect is the idea that an environmental tax, by raising prices, worsens the distortions already caused by income taxes.

facts.text: Bovenberg and Mooij argue that where an income tax already distorts labor supply, the best environmental tax is below the full Pigouvian level.
As consumers switch from the taxed dirty good to a clean one, the tax base and its revenue shrink, so income taxes cannot stay low.
Goulder, Parry and Burtraw agree that the net welfare effect of an environmental tax depends on the existing tax rate.

title: Second-best Pigouvian taxation
article: Pigouvian tax#Second-best optimal Pigouvian taxation (indirect taxation)

definition.text: Second-best Pigouvian taxation taxes a product linked to a harm when the harm itself cannot be taxed directly.

facts.text: For example, policymakers may tax gasoline instead of vehicle emissions.
Because people buy different amounts and drive vehicles in different states, the tax falls unevenly relative to the harm each causes.
Knittel and Sandler found such taxes an inefficient way to reduce vehicle emissions.

title: Measurement problem of Pigouvian taxes

definition.text: The measurement problem is the criticism that governments cannot know the true social cost of an externality, so they cannot set the right Pigouvian tax.

facts.text: Pigou and Friedrich Hayek both saw the assumption that government can price the harm as a weakness of the tax.
William Baumol argued that social costs are extraordinarily hard to measure, partly because many are psychological and individual.
Lobbying by polluters or by opponents can push the tax level below or above the best level.

contested_note: Critics from Pigou to Baumol doubt that the optimal tax level can ever be measured.

definition.text: A noise tax is a charge meant to limit noise pollution that disturbs nearby communities or wildlife.

facts.text: Most noise taxes concern aviation and urban infrastructure such as highway building.
France taxes commercial and non-commercial aircraft landing at its 10 busiest airports.

title: Plastic tax
article: Pigouvian tax#Plastic taxes (e.g. on plastic bags)

definition.text: A plastic tax charges for plastic use or plastic waste to cut waste and encourage recycling.

facts.text: Since 2021 the EU budget has collected a contribution from member states based on their non-recycled plastic packaging waste.
Ireland's €0.22 point-of-sale tax on plastic bags shifted shoppers toward other bags and cut plastic bags' share of litter.

definition.text: The polluter pays principle says that whoever causes pollution should pay for the damage it does to the environment.

facts.text: It has also been used to make polluters bear the cost of preventing pollution.
Economics supports it: assigning all costs of a decision, including pollution harm, to the decision-maker removes externalities and is a condition for Pareto efficiency.
It underpins policies such as ecotaxes, and cap-and-trade schemes apply it by making polluters buy allowances to cover their emissions.
It is principle 16 of the 1992 Rio Declaration, though not binding in all areas of international environmental law.
It is used in all the major US pollution laws, including the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act and Superfund.
Historian Jean-Baptiste Fressoz notes that paying compensation for pollution was already the rule favored by 19th-century industrialists.
It has been doubted where nobody knew a pollutant was dangerous when it was emitted, as with early industrial carbon dioxide.

definition.text: Carbon fee and dividend taxes fossil fuels for their carbon and pays the money back to everyone in equal per-person payments.

facts.text: The fee is charged where fuels enter the economy, such as the well, mine or port, and rises over time to give a predictable price signal.
A border adjustment charges imports from countries without an equivalent carbon fee.
Returning all net fees makes the scheme revenue-neutral, which appeals to those who do not want government to grow.
Paying out the revenue as a universal climate income largely offsets the higher prices a carbon tax causes.
As of July 2022 eight jurisdictions used a form of it, including Switzerland, Austria and several Canadian provinces.
Switzerland returns about two-thirds of its carbon tax revenue through health insurance bills, but a 2019 survey found only 11.8% of residents knew most funds were redistributed.
A 2021 study of Canada and Switzerland found that returning the money did little to make carbon taxes more popular.

definition.text: Environmental pricing reform, or ecological fiscal reform, adjusts market prices through taxes or subsidies so they reflect environmental costs and benefits.

facts.text: It responds to externalities: when prices leave out environmental costs, self-interested choices can harm the environment and distort the economy.
Each market-based instrument, such as ecotaxes, tradeable pollution permits or paying for ecological services, is one instance of it.
It can cover the whole economy or focus on one sector or one problem such as climate change.
Environmental tax reform began in the Nordic countries in the early 1990s and spread to the Netherlands, Germany and the United Kingdom.
IMF economists found that a tax 50% above or below marginal damage still captures about three quarters of the welfare gain, so broad coverage matters more than precision.
The World Bank reported carbon pricing revenue rose from under $30 billion in 2016 to more than $107 billion in 2025.

title: Prices versus quantities

definition.text: Price-based instruments such as taxes fix the price of pollution and let the amount vary, while quantity-based instruments such as cap-and-trade fix the amount and let the price vary.

facts.text: In theory the two give the same result when pollution and costs match expectations, but they diverge when they do not.
Emissions trading sets a limit and lets permits be traded among emitters, while a carbon tax sets a price.
A 2018 survey found 58% of leading economists agreed carbon taxes are better than cap-and-trade, and none disagreed.
With a cap, uncertain supply and demand make permit prices uncertain, and industry bears the cost of that volatility.
A tax's main drawback is that the environmental outcome, such as a limit on emissions, is not guaranteed.
Under a uniform tax the agency cannot pick winners and losers, which leaves less room for corruption.
A tax sets a unit price and the market sets the quantity; under cap and trade the authorities set the quantity and the market sets the price.
Cap and trade adjusts to inflation automatically and its price falls in recessions, acting as an automatic stabilizer.

contested_note: Economists have long disagreed on whether price or quantity instruments are better for cutting emissions.

definition.text: Revenue recycling means using the money raised by an environmental tax to cut other taxes or return it to people, rather than adding it to general spending.

facts.text: How the revenue is used greatly affects the economic cost of an environmental tax reform.
If revenue is not used to cut distorting taxes or is badly spent, the overall benefits fall quickly.
Recycling revenue makes a carbon tax revenue-neutral, for example by lowering income tax or paying citizens a dividend.
Using a tax's revenue to reduce other distorting taxes is what opens the possibility of a double dividend.
IMF authors warn that dedicated funds can lead governments to set rates by the fund's needs instead of by actual damage.
The UK Climate Change Levy dropped revenue recycling in 2010, sending the money to the Exchequer.

title: Fossil fuel subsidy reform
article: Environmental pricing reform#Fossil Fuel subsidy reform

definition.text: Fossil fuel subsidy reform removes subsidies that keep fossil fuel prices below their supply cost or below their full environmental cost.

facts.text: The IMF separates explicit subsidies, where consumer prices are below supply cost, from implicit ones, where prices omit environmental damage.
Explicit subsidies reached 1.3% of global GDP in 2022 and fell to 0.6% in 2024, the IMF estimated.
Removing fossil fuel subsidies counts as an implicit carbon price.
Phase-out is politically difficult.

definition.text: A deposit-refund system adds a surcharge when a product is bought and pays it back when the product or its packaging is returned.

facts.text: It works like a Pigouvian tax that is refunded once the product is returned, rewarding proper disposal.
Beverage containers are the usual case, but it is also used for batteries, tyres, motor oil, electronics and shipping pallets.
It discourages illegal dumping, eases monitoring and is hard to evade.
It can end up favoring single-use packaging over refillable systems, as in Germany.
It is said to rest on the principles of extended producer responsibility.

title: Carbon pricing on shipping

definition.text: Carbon pricing on shipping charges ships for the greenhouse gases they emit.

facts.text: Maritime transport makes up 3% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
A carbon price is meant to close the cost gap between heavy fuel oil and low-carbon fuels, breaking a stand-off where fuel suppliers and shipowners each wait for the other to move first.
In 2023 the EU Emissions Trading System was extended to shipping, and the International Maritime Organization set a goal of net-zero shipping emissions by around 2050.
An IMO pricing scheme would be the first global carbon pricing system; countries including China, Brazil and South Africa oppose it as unfair to developing countries.

contested_note: Stakeholders disagree over whether shipping carbon revenue should be spent within shipping or as general climate finance.

title: Energy Innovation and Carbon Dividend Act
article: Energy Innovation and Carbon Dividend Act of 2019

definition.text: The Energy Innovation and Carbon Dividend Act was a US House bill to charge a fee on carbon at the point of extraction and return the money to citizens.

facts.text: The fee would start at $15 per tonne of CO2-equivalent and rise each year by $10 or more.
It was based on the Citizens' Climate Lobby's carbon fee and dividend proposal.
It gained 86 cosponsors in 2019 but never got a vote.

notes: Excluded: a single US bill that was never passed; useful only as an example under Carbon fee and dividend.

sources.title: Energy Innovation and Carbon Dividend Act of 2019

title: Energy Tax Act

definition.text: The Energy Tax Act of 1978 was a US law using taxes and tax credits to cut oil and gas demand during the 1970s energy crisis.

facts.text: It gave tax credits for home solar, wind and geothermal energy and for business renewable equipment.
It created the Gas Guzzler Tax on passenger cars with low EPA-rated fuel economy, paid by the maker or importer.
Critics argue the tax helped SUVs dominate because trucks, SUVs and minivans were exempt.

notes: Excluded: single-country law; the Gas Guzzler Tax may serve as an example under Feebate or Energy tax.

definition.text: An energy tax is a tax that raises the price of energy, usually charged on the fuels themselves.

facts.text: Energy taxes are the most commonly used environmental taxes in the world.
They can be levied on producing, distributing or using energy, mainly fossil fuels and sometimes electricity.
Arguments for them include cutting fiscal deficits as well as reducing pollution.
A weakness is that they impose costs in reduced economic output and jobs.
Energy taxes and the removal of fossil fuel subsidies can be seen as pricing carbon implicitly, because they change fossil fuel prices.
A US BTU tax proposed in 1993 to tax fuels by heat content passed the House but was rejected by the Senate after heavy lobbying.

title: Pigou Club
article: List of supporters of Pigouvian taxes

definition.text: The Pigou Club is economist Gregory Mankiw's name for economists and commentators who have publicly backed higher Pigouvian taxes.

facts.text: Named after Arthur Cecil Pigou, it gathers modern economists who support a carbon tax to tackle climate change.
The Economist, The Washington Post editorial board, NPR's Planet Money and The New York Times have expressed support for Pigouvian policies.

notes: Excluded: a list page of supporters, not a concept; may serve as colour under Pigouvian tax.

sources.title: List of supporters of Pigouvian taxes

definition.text: A steering tax, or ecological incentive tax, is meant to change taxpayers' behaviour rather than to raise revenue.

facts.text: A Pigouvian tax is a special case of a steering tax aimed at a negative externality.
If the tax succeeds in changing behaviour, its revenue falls, so the steering aim and the revenue aim pull against each other.
Some, like the Swiss tax on volatile organic compounds, are fully paid back to the population, rewarding people who pollute less.
A Swiss study found a per-person refund is the most progressive way to return environmental tax revenue.

title: British Columbia carbon tax

definition.text: The British Columbia carbon tax, in force from 2008 until its repeal on 1 April 2025, taxed fossil fuels while cutting income and corporate taxes by about the same amount.

facts.text: It began at $10 per tonne of CO2e on 1 July 2008, the first such tax in North America, and was designed to be revenue-neutral.
It was collected at the point of retail sale, such as the gas pump, with a tax credit to protect low-income families.
The rate reached $40 per tonne in 2019 and $80 per tonne in 2024.
A 2013 review reported per-capita fossil fuel use down 17.4% while GDP growth kept pace with the rest of Canada.
A 2017 paper found a small but significant 0.74 percent annual employment increase over 2007–2013.
A 2021 counterfactual study found no significant negative impact on GDP and complete pass-through of the tax into energy prices.

contested_note: Critics argued that falling fuel use reflected cross-border shopping and a Vancouver gas levy rather than the tax.

title: Congestion pricing

definition.text: Congestion pricing charges users of crowded public goods, such as busy roads, higher prices at peak times to reduce overuse.

facts.text: It manages crowding by regulating demand rather than adding supply.
The theory is that drivers in a jam impose costs on one another that they do not pay; a price makes them cover this social cost.
It encourages people to shift trips to other times, places or substitutes such as public transport.
Singapore was first to price congestion on urban roads, in 1975, building on William Vickrey's 1963 call to price traffic on Pigou's welfare principle.
Road schemes take four forms: a cordon around a city centre, area-wide pricing, a city-centre toll ring, or pricing of a single corridor or facility.
A 2019 study found that without congestion pricing, Stockholm's air would have been 5 to 15 percent more polluted between 2006 and 2010.
It remains highly controversial with the public, mainly over fairness, effects on businesses and fears it is just another tax.
New York City became the first US city to adopt it, in 2025.

contested_note: Even advocates acknowledge practical limits, and public acceptance remains contested before and after schemes start.

title: Dividend

definition.text: A dividend is a share of a corporation's profits paid out to its shareholders.

facts.text: Profit that is not paid out is reinvested in the business as retained earnings.
In climate policy the word is borrowed for payments of carbon revenue to citizens, as in cap and dividend, where money from selling pollution credits is rebated to people.

notes: Excluded: corporate-finance concept only loosely related to this chapter; the climate-dividend sense is covered by Carbon fee and dividend and Revenue recycling.

title: Eco-tariff

definition.text: An eco-tariff, or environmental tariff, is a trade barrier such as an import or export tax used to reduce pollution.

facts.text: It targets goods with a large carbon footprint or goods from countries with lax environmental rules; a carbon tariff is one type.
Supporters say it could stop foreign countries gaining advantage from weak rules and bring trading partners' standards into line.
Critics argue it reduces trade without reaching the main sources of pollution, much of which arises within a country's own borders.
Developing countries fear it as green protectionism: using environmental goals as cover for shielding domestic industry.
Tariffs on imports alone can weaken export competitiveness and contribute to deindustrialisation.

contested_note: There is debate over whether freer international trade increases pollution or, by raising incomes, ends up reducing it.

definition.text: Effluent is wastewater from sewers or industrial outlets that flows into rivers, lakes or the sea, either treated or untreated.

facts.text: It can carry fats and oils, solvents, detergents, heavy metals and food waste from many industries.
Warm cooling-water effluent from power stations causes thermal pollution.
In the US the Clean Water Act requires a permit for every direct discharge of effluent into surface waters.

definition.text: An excise is a tax on a particular category of goods, usually charged when they are made for sale at home.

facts.text: Unlike a sales tax or VAT charged as a share of the price, an excise is usually a fixed amount per unit, falls on few products and is heavier.
It is an indirect tax: the producer pays it but is expected to pass it on to buyers through higher prices.
Tobacco, alcohol and fuel are its three main targets in most countries.
Excises can correct externalities by charging for costs that buyers or sellers impose on society but that prices leave out.
Excises are increasingly placed on polluting transport and on products that create hard-to-recycle waste.

definition.text: A feebate charges a fee on products with harmful side effects and uses the money to give rebates on cleaner alternatives.

facts.text: Feebates are usually revenue-neutral, with the fees paying for the rebates.
Arthur H. Rosenfeld coined the idea in the 1970s; it has mostly been used in transport and energy.
Car buyers discount future fuel costs heavily, so a feebate puts the cost into the purchase price where it is noticed.

definition.text: A hypothecated, or earmarked, tax is one whose revenue is set aside for a particular kind of spending.

facts.text: It departs from the usual practice of paying all government spending out of one consolidated fund.
In strong hypothecation the tax funds only that service and the service is funded only by that tax; otherwise it is weak.
Supporters cite transparency, trust and public acceptance of higher taxes when people see where the money goes.
Critics say spending should follow policy rather than revenue, and earmarking reduces fiscal flexibility.

definition.text: A landfill tax is a charge per tonne or per unit of volume that raises the cost of dumping waste in landfill.

facts.text: It can raise revenue, fund environmental mitigation, or deter landfilling by making better alternatives cheaper by comparison.
Landfilling is discouraged because of landfill gas from biodegradable waste, scarce sites, lost recyclable materials and local opposition.
The UK's landfill tax, introduced in 1996, was its first environmental tax.
By making landfill dearer it creates an incentive to recycle plastics.

definition.text: Optimal tax theory studies how to design taxes that do the most for overall social welfare within economic limits.

facts.text: Taxes are needed to fund public goods and redistribution, but most taxes distort behaviour by making the taxed activity less attractive.
The task is to raise the needed revenue and redistribution while causing as little distortion as possible.
Lump-sum taxes and Pigouvian taxes are thought to distort less; a Pigouvian tax moves consumption toward the efficient level.
Frank Ramsey (1927) proposed that each good's tax should depend on how sensitive its supply and demand are to price.
Optimal taxes should also be fair: equal tax for equal ability to pay, and more tax for those with more ability.

definition.text: Cost pass-through is the extent to which a business changes its prices when its own costs change.

facts.text: It is measured as a pass-through rate; firms may absorb part of a cost change (rate below 1.0) or amplify it (above 1.0).
When buyers must have a good whatever the price, the whole cost increase reaches consumers; when buyers would leave at any price rise, producers absorb it all.
Pass-through is higher when demand is less sensitive to price and supply more sensitive.
A 2021 study found British Columbia's carbon tax was passed fully into energy prices.

definition.text: A per unit, or specific, tax is a fixed amount charged on each unit of a good sold, such as cents per kilogram, whatever its price.

facts.text: Excise taxes fall into this category; by contrast an ad valorem tax is a fixed percentage of the product's value.
On a supply-and-demand graph it shifts the supply curve up by exactly the amount of the tax, parallel to the original curve.
For tobacco, specific taxes cut consumption well, while ad valorem taxes can push smokers to cheaper brands.

definition.text: A plastic bag ban or charge is a law that restricts or puts a price on the lightweight plastic bags handed out by shops.

facts.text: Charges and bans are the two most popular ways to phase bags out; as of 2018, 30 countries charged consumers and 27 had banned the bags.
A 2018 study found a five-cent tax on disposable bags cut their use by 40 percentage points.
Ireland's €0.15 levy in 2002 cut bag use by 90% within weeks.
Bans can raise use of unregulated paper or thicker plastic bags and feed black markets.

definition.text: Pollution pricing reform adjusts market prices to include directly measurable pollution, such as dust and exhaust from road vehicles.

facts.text: It differs from general ecotaxes, which are not tied to a short-term measurement of the impact.
Options include extra taxes on dirtier fuels, annual taxes on more polluting engine types, and daily traffic limits set by measured pollution.

definition.text: A regressive tax is one whose rate falls as the amount being taxed rises, so poorer people pay a larger share of what they have.

facts.text: A tax can also count as regressive when the taxed activity is done more by the poor than by the rich.
Its opposite, a progressive tax, takes a higher percentage from those with higher incomes.
Taxes on everyday essentials such as food, fuel, energy and housing, including carbon taxes, are often regressive.
Because spending on necessities like food barely rises with income, such taxes weigh most heavily on lower-income households.
Some governments give rebates to lower-income households to soften the effect.
A number of studies find a carbon tax without extra benefits or tax credits hits poor households harder than rich ones.

definition.text: Road pricing means charging drivers directly for road use, through tolls, distance or time fees, congestion charges or charges on more polluting vehicles.

facts.text: The charges may mainly raise money for roads or manage demand to cut congestion, pollution, noise and crashes.
William Vickrey built on Pigou's ideas to make the theoretical case for road pricing in the 1950s, proposing electronic charging for busy roads.
Distance-based lorry charges in Austria (2004) and Germany (2005) vary by emissions level and axles.
A Stockholm study found that without congestion pricing the city's air would have been five to ten percent more polluted in 2006–2010, with 45 percent more asthma attacks in young children.

conflicts.text: The Congestion pricing article reports the same Stockholm finding as 5 to 15 percent more polluted air.
conflicts.note: Two articles quote the same Stockholm 2006–2010 study with different upper bounds.

definition.text: A sin tax is an excise on goods and services seen as harmful, such as alcohol, tobacco, sugar, gambling or polluting vehicles.

facts.text: Unlike a Pigouvian tax, which charges for the damage done to others, a sin tax raises the price mainly to cut use.
Raising a sin tax is often more popular than raising other taxes.
Critics call sin taxes regressive and say they encourage smuggling and black markets.
A government may come to depend on the revenue and so need the 'sinful' behaviour to continue.

definition.text: A stormwater fee charges property owners for polluted rainwater runoff from their hard, waterproof surfaces.

facts.text: The charge grows with the area of roofs, driveways and paving that stop rain soaking into the ground.
In Germany builders install rain storage tanks and soakaways to lower the fee, raising rainwater recycling and cutting tap water use.
A 2023 study counted at least 2,100 stormwater utilities in 42 US states and the District of Columbia.
Maryland's 2012 fee, dubbed a 'rain tax', funded runoff controls to clean up the Chesapeake Bay but was made optional in 2015.

definition.text: A tax shift, or tax swap, cuts some taxes and raises others while keeping total revenue the same.

facts.text: It can mean a desired move toward socially efficient taxes such as ecotaxes and sin taxes.
A green tax shift raises taxes on pollution while lowering taxes such as income, payroll or property taxes.
Its aim is often 'full cost accounting', using fiscal policy to fold externalities into prices.
Tax shifts usually aim to stay revenue-neutral and keep the system progressive, protecting the most vulnerable.
British Columbia's carbon tax shift gave it one of Canada's lowest income tax rates as of 2012.

definition.text: A user fee is a payment charged to people for using a facility or service, such as a park, toll road or parking space.

facts.text: Fuel taxes that fund highways act as user fees: those who drive more pay more for roads.
Unlike broad taxes, user fees fall only on those who use the service.
Critics argue that fees for basic services in developing countries hurt the poorest most.

title: Citizens' Climate Lobby

definition.text: Citizens' Climate Lobby is an international grassroots group that trains volunteers to lobby elected representatives on climate policy.

facts.text: It proposes a fee on carbon dioxide and equivalent gases to cut US emissions.
Carbon fee and dividend is its preferred climate solution, and its chapters abroad push for a revenue-neutral version.

notes: Excluded: a single advocacy NGO; useful only as context under Carbon fee and dividend.
